title: Butterflies Crossed the Atlantic Nonstop on Fuel for a Fifth of the Trip

scenes.text: Butterflies crossed the Atlantic Ocean without landing once.
In 2013, a scientist found painted ladies on a beach in French Guiana, wings torn. That species doesn't live in the Americas.
They had come from Africa, over 4,200 kilometres of open water, in five to eight days.
scenes.keywords: painted lady butterfly close up wings

scenes.text: On their own fat they could fly about 780 kilometres. Not even a fifth of the way.
Pollen on their bodies came from two African plants. The winds that week blew straight across the ocean.
They glided on the wind and flapped only when they had to. A record for any insect, published in 2024.

description:
Butterflies crossed the Atlantic Ocean without landing once.
In October 2013 researcher Gerard Talavera found painted lady butterflies with torn wings on a beach in French Guiana, a species not found in South America. A 2024 study in Nature Communications used pollen DNA from two West African plants, genomes and wing isotopes to show they had flown over 4,200 kilometres of open ocean in five to eight days. Their fat reserves alone would carry them about 780 kilometres, so they survived by gliding on exceptionally favourable winds.
What is the longest journey you have seen an animal make?
first_comment: Some of them may have started in western Europe, which would make the whole trip 7,000 kilometres or more. Which animal migration impresses you most?
